data.cultural_impact: The name Lucilla carries an aura of brightness and clarity, suggesting a strong connection to light and the natural world. This name may evoke images of the radiant Roman goddess Lucca, who was the patron of the city of Lucca in Italy and presided over urban growth and prosperity. The name Lucilla has also been popular in various cultures throughout history, with notable bearers including a princess of the House of Bourbon and the sister of Queen Elizabeth I of England.
data.spiritual_significance: Lucilla is a name deeply rooted in spiritual traditions, with several saints bearing this name. The original Lucilla was a young Roman virgin who was martyred during the persecution of Christians under Emperor Maximian in 283 AD. She is believed to have maintained her faith in Christ despite being subjected to various forms of torture, and her courage and dedication to her beliefs continue to inspire followers today. Another St. Lucilla, an Italian noblewoman, devoted her life to caring for the sick and poor and was canonized in 1272. Lucilla's name reflects a connection to the light of God and the radiance of a pure and faithful spirit.

historical_references.reference: Lucilla, the wife of Emperor Maximian, was a prominent figure in the late Roman Empire during the 4th century AD. She is remembered for her patronage of Christian causes and her support of St. Ambrose, who became bishop of Milan in 374 AD. Lucilla's conversion to Christianity is believed to have influenced her husband, who later issued edicts that granted religious toleration to Christians in the empire.
historical_references.context: Patronage of Christianity and support for St. Ambrose

historical_references.reference: Lucilla of Syracuse, a martyr and saint in the early Christian Church, is believed to have lived during the 3rd or 4th century AD. Little is known about her life, but she is remembered for her bravery in the face of persecution under the Roman Emperor Diocletian, who issued edicts mandating the destruction of Christian churches and the execution of Christians. Lucilla is said to have been arrested and tortured, but refused to renounce her faith, and was eventually executed.
historical_references.time_period: Early Christian Church (3rd or 4th century AD)
historical_references.context: Martyrdom and persecution under Roman Emperor Diocletian
